concepts.title: The Node.js Event Loop & libuv
concepts.description: Node.js executes your JavaScript on a single thread, yet routinely serves thousands of concurrent connections without spawning a thread per request -- the event loop and the libuv library underneath it are the mechanism that makes this possible, and understanding them explains both Node's biggest strength and its single most common performance trap.
learningObjectives: Explain why Node.js can handle many concurrent I/O-bound operations despite running your JavaScript on a single thread.
Describe the role libuv and its thread pool play in offloading work that has no native asynchronous OS API.
List the event loop's main phases -- timers, poll, and check -- and identify what kind of callback runs in each.
Distinguish blocking (synchronous) calls from non-blocking (asynchronous) calls, and predict which one will stall every other request being served.
Predict the relative ordering of setTimeout, setImmediate, and process.nextTick callbacks in a given snippet.

sections.heading: One Thread, Many Connections
sections.body:
Every line of your own JavaScript in a Node.js process runs on exactly one thread -- the same thread, one call stack, one thing executing at a time, no exceptions. If that were the whole story, Node would be a poor choice for a server: a single web request that took even 200ms to handle would make every other concurrent client wait in line behind it. That is not what actually happens in practice, and the reason is that Node deliberately separates 'running your JavaScript' from 'waiting on I/O.' When your code calls something like a database query, a file read, or an HTTP request to another service, Node does not sit there spinning the CPU waiting for the answer. It hands the request off -- to the operating system's networking stack, or to libuv (covered below) -- and immediately returns control to your single thread so it can go do other work: handle another incoming request, run a timer, respond to a different client entirely. When the I/O operation eventually finishes, its result is placed on a queue, and the event loop picks it up and runs your callback for it, on that same single thread, at the next opportunity.

This is why Node is described as good at I/O-bound workloads and bad at CPU-bound ones. A server that spends most of its time waiting -- for a database, a disk, another network service -- can have hundreds of those waits in flight simultaneously, because 'waiting' costs no CPU time on your thread at all; the waiting happens elsewhere, outside your JavaScript entirely. But a server that spends its time actually computing -- resizing images, running a complex regex over megabytes of text, computing a hash -- has no such trick available, because that work has to happen as JavaScript instructions on your one thread, and nothing else can run while it does. If you have genuinely CPU-heavy work, the real fix is not 'understand the event loop harder' -- it's to move that work off the main thread entirely, using worker_threads (a separate JS thread with its own event loop) or a child process, or offloading it to another service. The event loop model doesn't parallelize your CPU-bound code; it just makes sure that code isn't blocking anyone unless you write it in a way that does.

sections.heading: libuv and the Thread Pool
sections.body:
The event loop itself, plus a good deal of what makes non-blocking I/O possible, is implemented by a C library called **libuv**, which Node is built on top of. libuv gives Node two different strategies for turning slow operations into non-blocking ones, and which strategy applies depends on what kind of operation it is -- this distinction trips up a lot of people who assume 'async I/O' is one uniform mechanism.

For network I/O -- TCP sockets, which is what HTTP servers and most databases sit on top of -- the operating system itself provides genuinely asynchronous, event-driven APIs (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows). libuv talks to these directly: it asks the OS to notify it when a socket has data ready, and does something else in the meantime. No extra thread is spun up per socket; the waiting is handled by the kernel, and libuv just polls for what's ready now as part of the event loop's poll phase (see the next section).

File system operations are a different story. Most operating systems' file APIs are fundamentally blocking at the OS level -- there is no equivalent of epoll for 'tell me when this file read is done' on most platforms the way there is for sockets. So for fs operations (and a handful of other things: some crypto functions like pbkdf2 and scrypt, DNS lookups via dns.lookup, and some zlib compression calls), libuv fakes non-blocking behavior by handing the actual blocking call off to a **worker thread pool** -- a fixed-size pool of background OS threads, four by default, controlled by the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable. The blocking call runs to completion on one of those background threads (genuinely blocking *that* thread, just not your main JS thread), and when it finishes, its result is queued back for your callback to run on the main thread.

This has a real, practical consequence worth remembering: the thread pool is small (four threads by default) and shared across every fs/crypto/dns/zlib operation your whole app issues. If you kick off, say, twenty CPU-heavy crypto.pbkdf2 password hashes at once, only four run genuinely in parallel; the other sixteen queue up waiting for a free thread, even though your main JS thread is sitting completely idle the whole time. This is a common, confusing performance cliff -- 'my server has plenty of idle CPU cores, why are my password hashes queuing up?' -- and the answer is almost always: the libuv thread pool size, not the number of CPU cores or the main thread, is the bottleneck for that specific class of operation.

sections.heading: The Phases of the Event Loop
sections.body:
The event loop is not one undifferentiated queue -- it's a fixed cycle of distinct **phases**, each responsible for a different category of callback, run in the same order every single iteration (or 'tick') of the loop. The phases that matter most day to day are:

1. **timers** -- runs callbacks scheduled by setTimeout and setInterval whose delay has elapsed.
2. **pending callbacks** -- runs certain I/O callbacks deferred from the previous loop iteration (mostly some error cases you'll rarely touch directly).
3. **poll** -- the workhorse phase: retrieves new I/O events (a socket became readable, a file read finished) and runs their callbacks. If there's nothing else scheduled, the loop will actually sit here and block, waiting for something to happen, rather than spinning the CPU for no reason -- this is what lets an idle Node process use roughly 0% CPU while still serving connections.
4. **check** -- runs setImmediate callbacks, specifically *after* the poll phase has finished for this iteration.
5. **close callbacks** -- runs close-event handlers, e.g. socket.on('close', ...).

One detail explains a huge fraction of 'why did that run in that order' confusion: **process.nextTick and resolved Promises are not phases of the event loop at all.** They're drained from separate microtask-style queues *between every single callback*, not just between phases -- process.nextTick's queue is checked (and fully drained) first, then the Promise microtask queue, and only once both are completely empty does Node move on to whatever's next, whether that's the next callback in the current phase or the next phase entirely. That's why process.nextTick(fn) and Promise.resolve().then(fn) reliably run before *any* timer or I/O callback, no matter how small a delay you give setTimeout -- they cut in line ahead of the whole phase-based loop, every time.

A classic, genuinely useful ordering puzzle to build intuition: setTimeout(fn, 0) vs setImmediate(fn), called at the top level of your program (not inside an I/O callback). Their relative order is technically **not guaranteed** here, because it depends on timing details of process startup that can vary run to run. But call them from *inside* an I/O callback -- say, inside an fs.readFile callback, which itself runs during the poll phase -- and the order becomes deterministic: setImmediate will always fire before the setTimeout(fn, 0), because the loop is already in the poll phase; it proceeds directly to the check phase next (running the setImmediate callback), and only reaches the timers phase on the *next* full iteration of the loop.

sections.heading: Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O -- and Why It's the Cardinal Sin
sections.body:
Every core I/O API in Node ships in (at least) two flavors: a blocking, synchronous version, usually suffixed Sync (fs.readFileSync, fs.writeFileSync), and a non-blocking, asynchronous version (fs.readFile with a callback, or fs.promises.readFile). The synchronous version does exactly what its name says: it blocks -- the entire single JS thread stops and waits, doing absolutely nothing else, until that one operation completes. No other request is served, no timer fires, no other callback runs -- the whole process is frozen for the duration of that call.

That's a completely reasonable thing to do in a one-off script, or during application startup before you've begun accepting traffic -- reading a config file synchronously before app.listen() is fine, because there's no concurrent traffic to stall yet. It becomes a serious bug the moment it happens inside code that runs *per request* in a server meant to serve many clients concurrently: one client's request now stalls every other client's request for as long as that synchronous call takes, completely defeating the concurrency model this whole runtime is built around. This is, without exaggeration, one of the single most common ways real Node servers get slow under load, and it's often invisible in local testing with one browser tab open, because with only one 'client,' there's nothing else waiting to be blocked.

It's worth being explicit that 'non-blocking' specifically means I/O -- waiting on a network response, a disk read, a timer. It does **not** mean 'safe from ever stalling the loop.' A synchronous, CPU-heavy computation -- a huge JSON.parse of a multi-megabyte payload, a poorly written regular expression suffering catastrophic backtracking, a tight loop doing real work over a large array -- blocks the event loop exactly as thoroughly as fs.readFileSync does, and there is no asynchronous version of 'do less CPU work' to reach for. The fix for I/O is to use the non-blocking API; the fix for genuinely heavy computation is to either make it faster, break it into chunks yielded back to the event loop, or move it off the main thread with worker_threads.

examples.title: Blocking the Event Loop with a Synchronous Call
examples.explanation: If one client requests /report while a large file is being read synchronously, every other client -- even one hitting the trivially cheap '/' route -- has to wait for that entire read to finish before getting a response, because there is only one thread and it is fully occupied. Under a single manual test with one browser tab this looks completely fine, since there's nothing else competing for the thread; the problem only becomes visible under real concurrent load, which is exactly why this class of bug survives so often into production. The fix is to swap fs.readFileSync for fs.readFile (callback) or fs.promises.readFile (awaited in an async handler) -- either lets the event loop keep serving other requests while libuv's thread pool handles the actual disk read in the background.

examples.title: setImmediate vs setTimeout Inside an I/O Callback
examples.explanation: Because both calls happen inside an I/O callback -- which itself runs during the poll phase -- the ordering here is deterministic, unlike the same two calls made at the top level of a script. Once the poll phase finishes processing this callback, the event loop moves directly on to the check phase, where setImmediate's callback is waiting, and runs it. Only on a *later* pass through the full cycle does the loop reach the timers phase, where the setTimeout callback finally gets its turn. So 'immediate' always prints before 'timeout' here, specifically because of where in the phase cycle the surrounding code happens to be running -- the same two calls made outside any I/O callback would not have this guarantee.

examples.title: process.nextTick, Promises, and setTimeout: Full Ordering
examples.explanation: All synchronous code runs to completion first, top to bottom, before any queued callback gets a turn at all -- that's why 'start' and 'end' print immediately, in that order, regardless of what was scheduled in between them. Once the synchronous code finishes, Node fully drains the process.nextTick queue before even glancing at the Promise microtask queue, so 'nextTick' prints next. Only once that queue is completely empty does Node drain the microtask queue, printing 'promise'. Only once *both* of those queues are fully empty does the event loop actually move into the timers phase and run the setTimeout callback, printing 'timeout' last. This ordering -- nextTick, then microtasks, then the phase-based event loop -- is fixed and worth memorizing, because it's the exact source of most 'why did this run before that' surprises in real code.

misconceptions.description: Node.js being 'single-threaded' means it can only ever do one thing at a time, including I/O -- so lots of concurrent requests must secretly be queued up and handled one after another.
misconceptions.clarification: JavaScript execution is single-threaded, but I/O work itself is delegated to the operating system's asynchronous facilities or to libuv's thread pool, both of which genuinely run concurrently, outside that one JS thread entirely. Only the (typically tiny) work of running your callback in response to a finished I/O operation is scheduled onto the single thread, one callback at a time. That's why a server juggling many concurrent slow database calls can still feel snappy: the actual waiting is not consuming your one thread's time at all -- it's happening elsewhere, and your thread is free to handle other callbacks in the meantime.

misconceptions.description: setTimeout(fn, 0) means fn runs immediately, essentially at time zero, ahead of anything else.
misconceptions.clarification: Modern Node clamps the minimum timer delay to 1ms, but even that isn't the main point: 'immediately' in the strongest sense -- before anything else at all -- is closer to what process.nextTick does, not setTimeout. Regardless of the delay you pass, a setTimeout callback still has to wait for the current synchronous code to finish completely, for the process.nextTick queue to fully drain, for the Promise microtask queue to fully drain, and for the event loop to actually reach the timers phase on a subsequent iteration. Even process.nextTick doesn't preempt currently-executing synchronous code -- it just jumps the queue ahead of timers and I/O callbacks once that code finishes.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and in what order? Explain why.
hints: Synchronous code -- anything not inside a callback -- always finishes running first, top to bottom, before any queued callback gets a turn.
Once the synchronous code is done, Node fully drains the process.nextTick queue before it even looks at the Promise microtask queue.
Only after both the nextTick queue AND the microtask queue are completely empty does the event loop move on to the timers phase, where the setTimeout callback is waiting.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 1: start, 5: end, 4: nextTick, 3: promise, 2: timeout -- in that order.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two console.log calls that aren't inside any callback ('1: start' and '5: end') are plain synchronous code, so they run first and in the order they textually appear, regardless of what gets scheduled in between them. Once that synchronous code finishes, Node drains the process.nextTick queue completely before touching anything else, so '4: nextTick' prints next. Only after that queue is empty does Node drain the Promise microtask queue, printing '3: promise'. Only once both of those queues are fully empty does the event loop proceed into the timers phase and run the setTimeout callback, printing '2: timeout' last of all.

exercises.prompt: This HTTP server is meant to serve an instant response on '/' even while a slower '/report' request involving a large file read is in flight for another client. In testing with two simultaneous clients, the '/' request is unexpectedly delayed until the '/report' request finishes. Find and fix the bug.
hints: fs.readFileSync does exactly what its name says -- while it blocks, who else is affected besides the client that requested /report?
Node has more than one API for reading a file. Which one lets the event loop keep handling other requests while the read is in progress?
Look for a callback-based or Promise-based fs API, and remember your handler function itself will need to become async (or accept a callback) to use it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: fs.readFileSync blocks the entire single JS thread for the duration of the read -- while it runs, absolutely nothing else can happen, including handling the concurrent '/' request, regardless of which client asked for the slow route. Switching to fs/promises's readFile (non-blocking, handled via libuv's thread pool under the hood) and awaiting it inside an async request handler lets the event loop keep servicing the '/' request -- and everyone else -- while the file read for '/report' happens in the background. The main thread only re-engages with that specific request once the data is actually ready, exactly the concurrency model Node is designed around.

assessments.prompt: A Node.js server issues twenty concurrent crypto.pbkdf2 password-hashing calls (a CPU-heavy operation Node routes through libuv's thread pool). The machine has 16 idle CPU cores. What should you actually expect?
options: All twenty run fully in parallel immediately, since there are far more CPU cores than operations.
Only as many run in parallel as there are threads in libuv's thread pool (four by default) -- the rest queue, waiting for a free thread, regardless of how many CPU cores are idle.
None of them can run until the main JS thread is completely idle, since libuv borrows the main thread for CPU-heavy work.
They run one at a time, always, because pbkdf2 blocks the event loop directly.
assessments.explanation: libuv's thread pool defaults to four threads (controlled by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), and that fixed pool size -- not the number of available CPU cores -- is the bottleneck for operations routed through it, so at most four of the twenty pbkdf2 calls run genuinely in parallel at any moment; the rest queue for a free thread. Option A is wrong because idle CPU cores are irrelevant unless UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is explicitly raised to make use of them. Option C is wrong: the thread pool is separate from the main JS thread and doesn't require it to be idle to make progress. Option D is wrong because pbkdf2 is precisely one of the operations libuv offloads to the thread pool *so that* it does not block the event loop, and the pool does allow some real parallelism (four at once), not strictly one at a time.

assessments.prompt: Node's TCP/network I/O does not need libuv's worker thread pool, while file system operations do. What actually explains this difference?
options: Network I/O is inherently faster than disk I/O, so it never needs a background thread regardless of the OS.

Operating systems provide genuinely asynchronous, event-driven APIs for sockets (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows) that libuv can hook into directly, but most OS file APIs are fundamentally blocking, so libuv offloads those calls to background threads in the pool instead.
Node maintains a separate, larger thread pool exclusively for network sockets that isn't governed by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.
File system operations are handled directly in the poll phase, bypassing the thread pool entirely, while network operations always use the thread pool.
assessments.explanation: The distinction comes down to what the underlying operating system actually offers. For sockets, the OS itself provides non-blocking, event-driven notification mechanisms, so libuv just asks to be told when a socket is ready and does other work meanwhile -- no extra thread needed. Most file APIs have no equivalent 'notify me when ready' mechanism at the OS level, so libuv fakes non-blocking behavior for fs calls by running the genuinely blocking call on a background thread from its fixed pool. Option A is wrong -- relative speed isn't the mechanism at play. Option C is wrong -- there is no separate socket-specific thread pool; sockets don't need the thread pool at all. Option D is wrong -- it inverts which category actually uses the thread pool.

assessments.prompt: An I/O callback is currently running during the poll phase. Partway through, it calls process.nextTick(fn) once. Relative to the event loop's next callback (whether that's the next poll-phase callback or the check phase), when does fn actually run?
options: Immediately after the current callback finishes, before the event loop moves on to anything else at all -- process.nextTick's queue is drained between every single callback, not just between phases.
Only after the poll phase entirely finishes and the check phase begins.
Only on the next full iteration of the event loop, after every phase has had a turn.
At a genuinely unpredictable time, since nextTick provides no ordering guarantee relative to other callbacks.
assessments.explanation: process.nextTick's queue (along with the Promise microtask queue right after it) is checked and fully drained between every single callback, not merely between the event loop's phases -- so fn runs immediately once the current I/O callback finishes, before the loop proceeds to whatever callback would normally run next, even if that next callback is still within the very same poll phase. Option B and C both describe a phase-based or iteration-based deferral, which is exactly what nextTick bypasses. Option D is wrong -- nextTick's ordering relative to other callbacks is a fixed, reliable guarantee, not an unpredictable one.

assessments.prompt: A developer replaces a blocking fs.readFileSync call with fs.promises.readFile inside a request handler, but the server still stalls under concurrent load whenever a request triggers JSON.parse on a very large payload already in memory. What best explains this?
options: fs.promises.readFile doesn't actually use libuv's thread pool, so it's just as blocking as the Sync version was.

JSON.parse is itself a synchronous, CPU-bound operation running entirely on the main JS thread -- non-blocking APIs solve blocking I/O specifically, not CPU-heavy computation, which still monopolizes the single thread for as long as it takes to run.
The event loop's poll phase automatically blocks whenever any JSON parsing occurs, regardless of payload size.
Switching to fs.promises.readFile made things worse, because it always runs on a separate thread that contends with JSON.parse for CPU time.
assessments.explanation: 'Non-blocking' specifically refers to I/O -- waiting on a disk, a network response, a timer -- not to CPU-heavy computation. A large JSON.parse call is ordinary synchronous JavaScript that runs to completion on the single main thread, blocking every other request exactly as thoroughly as a synchronous I/O call would, and switching the file read to a non-blocking API does nothing to change that, since the read was never the bottleneck in this scenario. Option A is wrong -- fs.promises.readFile is genuinely non-blocking. Option C is wrong -- the poll phase has no special-cased blocking behavior tied to JSON parsing. Option D is wrong -- fs.promises.readFile's I/O work happens via the thread pool, but the CPU-bound JSON.parse call itself still runs on the main thread regardless.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'Node.js is single-threaded, so our server can only truly handle one request at a time -- the concurrency everyone talks about is really just an illusion created by interleaving.' Explain what's right and what's misleading about this claim, using the event loop and libuv to justify your answer.
assessments.modelAnswer: The literal, narrow part of the claim is true: JavaScript execution in Node really is single-threaded, and at any given instant, only one JS callback is actually running -- that part is not an illusion. Where the claim goes wrong is in equating 'running JS' with 'handling a request.' For a typical I/O-bound request -- one that queries a database, reads a file, or calls another service -- the overwhelming majority of that request's wall-clock lifetime is spent waiting, not computing, and that waiting is delegated either to the operating system's asynchronous socket facilities or to libuv's thread pool, both of which run genuinely concurrently, entirely outside the single JS thread. That means hundreds of requests really can be simultaneously 'in flight,' waiting on their own I/O, at essentially zero cost to the one JS thread, which is only needed for the comparatively tiny slices of actual work -- parsing input, deciding what to do, building a response -- that each request requires. Those slices do run one at a time, interleaved by the event loop, but because they're small relative to the waiting time, the system as a whole behaves like real concurrency for I/O-bound workloads, not a mere illusion; the bottleneck resource (the single JS thread) is rarely the busy one. Where the teammate's framing becomes literally correct, though, is for CPU-bound workloads: if a request requires substantial computation rather than waiting on I/O, there's nothing to delegate, and that computation genuinely does run to completion on the one thread, blocking every other request for its entire duration -- which is exactly why real CPU-heavy work should be moved to worker_threads or a separate process rather than handled inline.

concepts.title: Callbacks, Promises, and Async/Await in Node
concepts.description: Node's asynchronous story evolved in three layers -- raw error-first callbacks, then Promises, then async/await syntax on top of Promises -- and while all three ultimately schedule work through the same event loop, they differ sharply in how errors propagate, how well they compose, and how easy they make it to accidentally write a subtly broken program.
learningObjectives: Write and correctly consume a Node-style error-first callback, checking the error argument before touching any result.
Explain what 'callback hell' actually costs beyond indentation -- specifically around error handling and composability.
Convert a callback-based API to a Promise-based one using util.promisify, and know when a Promise-native version already exists.
Use async/await with try/catch to write asynchronous logic that reads top-to-bottom, and explain what an async function actually returns.
Identify the bug caused by forgetting to await a Promise inside an async function, including how it can produce an unhandled promise rejection.

sections.heading: The Original Pattern: Error-First Callbacks
Callback Hell, and Why It's a Real Engineering Problem, Not Just Ugly Indentation
Promises: A Value That Represents a Future Result
sections.body:
A **Promise** is an object representing a value that may not exist yet, but will (eventually) either resolve successfully or reject with an error. Every Promise is in exactly one of three states at any moment: **pending** (still waiting), **fulfilled** (resolved with a value), or **rejected** (failed with a reason) -- and once it leaves pending, it never changes state again. You attach a handler for the eventual success value with .then(value => ...), for the eventual failure with .catch(err => ...), and for 'run this regardless of outcome' with .finally(() => ...).

The critical improvement over raw callbacks is that .then() calls **chain**, and a single .catch() at the end of a chain catches a rejection from *any* step earlier in that chain -- you don't need a separate error check duplicated at every level:

```javascript
const fs = require('fs/promises');

fs.readFile('./user-id.txt', 'utf8')
  .then(id => db.getUser(id.trim()))
  .then(user => db.getOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders => fs.writeFile('./orders.json', JSON.stringify(orders)))
  .then(() => console.log('Done.'))
  .catch(err => handleError(err));
```

This reads top to bottom as a flat pipeline instead of a nested pyramid, and one .catch() handles a failure from *any* of the four steps -- there's no way for an error to slip through unhandled the way a missed if (err) check could before. For code that still exposes an old-style callback API (either in Node core, or in an older third-party library), util.promisify(fn) wraps it into a function that returns a Promise instead of taking a callback, assuming that function follows the standard (err, result) convention -- though these days, most of Node's own core modules already ship a ready-made Promise-based variant directly (fs.promises, or require('node:fs/promises')), so reaching for util.promisify by hand is increasingly rare outside of older third-party callback APIs.

sections.heading: async/await: The Same Promises, Read as Straight-Line Code

examples.title: Correctly Consuming an Error-First Callback
examples.explanation: The if (err) return; guard is doing real work, not just being defensive for its own sake: if the file genuinely doesn't exist, err will be a real Error object and contents will be undefined. Without the guard, the code would fall through to JSON.parse(undefined), which throws its own, unrelated-looking error ('Unexpected token u in JSON at position 0') that has nothing to do with the actual root cause (a missing file) -- exactly the kind of confusing, misleading error message that makes debugging callback code painful. Checking err first and returning immediately means the real cause of failure is the one that gets reported.

examples.title: Fixing an Unhandled Rejection Caused by a Missing await
examples.explanation: Because await is missing, user is bound to the Promise object that db.getUser(userId) returns, not to the eventual user record -- so user.orders is undefined (Promises don't have an orders property), and reading .length off that throws a TypeError immediately, on the very next line. In this particular example the mistake still surfaces relatively loudly because getUserOrderCount's own returned Promise rejects, and the caller happens to have a .catch() attached to log it. If no code anywhere had attached a .catch() or try/catch to this call chain, that same TypeError would instead become a silent, unhandled promise rejection -- which, on modern Node, terminates the process outright rather than merely printing a warning. The fix is simply adding the missing await in front of db.getUser(userId).

examples.title: Sequential vs Parallel awaits with Promise.all
examples.explanation: Both functions are syntactically valid async/await code with no missing awaits and no bugs in the sense of 'wrong output' -- they produce the same final array of results. The difference is purely about timing: the sequential version's for...of loop awaits each call before even starting the next one, so three network round trips happen back-to-back, one after another. The parallel version calls db.getOrders for every id immediately, with no awaiting in between, so all three requests are in flight concurrently the moment the function runs, and Promise.all simply waits for the slowest one to finish. When the operations are genuinely independent of each other, the sequential version is wasting real wall-clock time for no correctness benefit -- but if a later request actually depended on an earlier one's result, sequential awaiting would be the only correct option, not just an incidental style choice.

misconceptions.description: Marking a function async makes it run on a separate thread, in parallel with the rest of the program.
misconceptions.clarification: async is Promise syntax sugar only -- it introduces no new threads and no new concurrency mechanism. An async function's own synchronous statements still execute on the single main thread, in order, exactly like any other function; the only reason execution can appear to 'jump away' to other code is that hitting an await genuinely pauses that specific function and hands control back to the event loop, which may then run something else while waiting. Concurrency only ever comes from operations that do real I/O yielding control back to the event loop, never from the async keyword itself creating threads or parallel execution of your JS.

misconceptions.description: await pauses the entire program -- it blocks the event loop until the Promise resolves.
misconceptions.clarification: await only suspends the one async function it's written in; the event loop keeps right on running everything else -- other timers, other I/O callbacks, other async functions' continuations -- while that particular function waits its turn to resume. It's cooperative, local suspension of a single call, not a global freeze, which is exactly the point: if await genuinely blocked the whole event loop, it would defeat the entire purpose of using non-blocking, asynchronous I/O in the first place, and would be no better than the Sync functions covered in the previous concept.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to fetch a 'user' for each id and log them in order, using Array.prototype.forEach. What does it actually print, and why doesn't it wait for each fetch to finish before starting the next?
hints: forEach calls its callback function once per element -- but does it do anything at all with what that callback function returns?
The callback passed to forEach here is itself an async function, so it returns a Promise every time it's called. forEach ignores that return value completely -- it never awaits it.

Because forEach fires off all three async callbacks without waiting between them, they all start their setTimeout timers at roughly the same moment -- so whichever one has the SHORTEST delay logs first, not whichever one started first.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'done looping' prints first, immediately, followed by 'user-3', 'user-2', 'user-1' in that order (shortest delay first) -- NOT 'user-1', 'user-2', 'user-3' in id order, and not after 'done looping' waits for anything.
exercises.solutionExplanation: forEach invokes its callback once per element but never looks at, awaits, or does anything with the Promise that async callback returns -- it just fires all three calls back to back, synchronously, with no waiting in between. Each call immediately starts its own setTimeout timer (100 - id*10 ms: 90ms, 80ms, 70ms respectively) and then forEach itself returns, letting printUsers's synchronous body continue straight on to console.log('done looping'), which runs before any of the timers have had a chance to fire. Once the timers do start completing, the shortest one (id=3, 70ms) resolves first, so 'user-3' logs first, then 'user-2' at 80ms, then 'user-1' at 90ms -- the exact reverse of what a naive reading of the loop suggests. The fix, if sequential in-order processing was intended, is a plain for...of loop (which genuinely awaits each iteration before starting the next) or, if order doesn't matter but waiting for all of them does, Promise.all(ids.map(...)).

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to return the total number of orders across several users, fetched from a slow database call. It's supposed to run all the lookups concurrently, since they don't depend on each other, but profiling shows it takes roughly three times longer than a single lookup for three users -- meaning it's actually running them one at a time. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at where await appears relative to the loop. Does the loop start the next iteration's request before or after the current one finishes?
await inside a for...of loop pauses that entire loop at every single iteration -- it will not move to the next id until the current db.getOrders call has fully resolved.
You want to START every request first, all at once, without waiting yet, collect all the resulting Promises, and only then wait for all of them together.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original loop awaits db.getOrders(id) on every single iteration, which means the next iteration's call isn't even made until the current one has completely resolved -- three sequential round trips, one after another, hence roughly 3x the latency of a single call. The fix separates 'starting' the requests from 'waiting' for them: userIds.map(id => db.getOrders(id)) calls db.getOrders for every id immediately, back to back, with no awaiting in between, producing an array of Promises that are all already in flight concurrently. Promise.all takes that whole array and returns a single Promise that resolves once every one of them has resolved (or rejects as soon as any one of them rejects), so the total wait time is roughly the duration of the single slowest lookup, not the sum of all of them.

assessments.prompt: What does calling an async function that has no explicit return statement, and that never throws, actually give you?
options: undefined, exactly like a normal non-async function with no return statement.
A Promise that resolves with the value undefined.
A Promise that stays pending forever, since nothing was explicitly returned.
A SyntaxError, because async functions require an explicit return statement.
assessments.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, no matter what happens inside its body -- if it falls off the end without an explicit return <value>, that Promise resolves with undefined, exactly mirroring how a plain function with no return statement evaluates to undefined on every call, except now wrapped in a Promise. Option A is the answer you'd get for the same code MINUS the async keyword -- adding async is precisely what changes the answer. Option C is wrong: falling off the end of a function body is not the same as never settling; the function still completes normally, it just resolves with undefined rather than something else. Option D is wrong -- async functions are completely allowed to omit return; it's common and valid whenever the function's purpose is a side effect rather than producing a value.

assessments.prompt: Why do Node's core APIs pass an error as the first argument to a callback instead of simply throwing when something goes wrong during an asynchronous operation?
options: Throwing inside an asynchronous callback would work fine; Node's designers preferred passing errors as data purely for stylistic consistency across the API.

By the time an asynchronous operation actually completes and its callback runs, the original call stack -- including any try/catch that wrapped the initial call -- is long gone, so there is no meaningful place for a thrown error to be caught; passing the error as an argument to a callback guaranteed to run works regardless of timing.
JavaScript did not support throw statements inside callback functions until ES2015, so early Node had no choice.
Passing errors as a callback argument avoids the performance cost of constructing an Error object.
assessments.explanation: A synchronous try/catch relies on the calling stack frame still being alive when the error occurs -- but an asynchronous callback runs long after the function that scheduled it has already returned, so that original stack frame, and any try/catch surrounding it, no longer exists to catch a thrown error. Node's core APIs sidestep this entirely by handing the error to the one function guaranteed to run when the operation finishes: your callback, as data in its first parameter. Option A understates that there's a real technical reason, not just style. Option C is factually wrong -- throw has always been part of JavaScript, including inside callbacks; the problem is about stack lifetime, not syntax availability. Option D is not the actual motivation; the cost of constructing an Error object plays no role in this convention's origin.

assessments.prompt: A developer claims: 'Marking a function async makes its body run on a separate thread, so several async functions execute their code in true parallel.' What's wrong with this claim?
options: Nothing -- this is exactly how async functions behave in Node.

async is Promise syntax sugar only; it creates no new threads. An async function's synchronous statements still run on the single main thread in the usual order, one at a time -- execution only appears to 'jump away' because hitting an await pauses that specific function and hands control back to the event loop, which may run other code while it waits.
async functions do run on separate threads, but only during the specific line where an I/O operation is awaited, not during ordinary synchronous statements.
async functions run on libuv's worker thread pool, the same pool used for fs and crypto operations.
assessments.explanation: The async keyword only changes what a function returns (always a Promise) and grants access to await inside its body -- it introduces no new concurrency mechanism and no new thread. Every synchronous statement in an async function's body still executes on the single main JS thread, in order, exactly like any other function; the illusion of 'jumping away' comes entirely from await voluntarily pausing that one function and returning control to the event loop, which is free to run other pending work in the meantime. Options C and D both invent a thread-based mechanism that doesn't exist -- await never hands JS execution off to another thread, whether during I/O or otherwise; the I/O itself may be handled elsewhere (by the OS or libuv's pool), but the async function's own JS code never runs anywhere but the main thread.

assessments.prompt: On Node 15 and later, what happens by default when a Promise rejects and nothing in the program -- no .catch(), no surrounding try/catch around an await -- ever handles that rejection?
options: Node silently discards the rejection; nothing is logged and the process continues normally.
Node logs a DeprecationWarning to the console, but the process keeps running exactly as it did on older Node versions.
The process crashes and exits, because Node's default behavior for an unhandled promise rejection changed from merely warning to actually terminating the process.
The rejected Promise is automatically retried up to three times before Node gives up and logs an error.
assessments.explanation: Earlier Node versions just printed a warning for an unhandled promise rejection and kept running. Starting with Node 15, the default behavior escalated: an unhandled rejection now terminates the process outright, on the reasoning that an error nobody was prepared to handle likely represents a real bug that shouldn't be allowed to fail silently. This is exactly why a single missing await -- which can produce an unhandled rejection if the un-awaited Promise later rejects -- can turn into a production crash rather than a quiet warning. Options A and B describe older or nonexistent behavior; option D describes a retry mechanism that Promises have no built-in concept of at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to a developer new to Node, why forgetting the await keyword on a Promise-returning call inside an async function is a common and often dangerous bug, and how the mistake can eventually surface as an 'unhandled promise rejection' crash.
assessments.modelAnswer: When you call a function that returns a Promise but don't put await in front of it inside an async function, the call still happens -- the asynchronous operation genuinely starts -- but the variable you assigned the result to is bound immediately to the Promise object itself, not to whatever value that Promise will eventually resolve with, because execution didn't pause to wait for it. Any code right after that line which assumes it has the real resolved value -- reading a property off it, passing it somewhere expecting a plain object -- is now operating on a Promise instead, which typically produces undefined for property lookups or an outright TypeError, in a way that's often confusing because the error appears to be about the wrong thing (a missing property) rather than about a missing await. The deeper danger shows up when that abandoned Promise later rejects with an error. Because nothing in the code ever attached a .catch() or wrapped the (missing) await in a try/catch, there's genuinely no handler anywhere waiting to receive that rejection -- it becomes what Node calls an 'unhandled promise rejection.' In recent Node versions (15 and later), Node's default behavior for this situation escalated from merely printing a warning to actually terminating the process, on the theory that an error nobody is prepared to handle probably represents a real bug that shouldn't be allowed to fail silently. So a single missing await can go from 'looks like it worked, mostly' in casual testing, to an outright process crash in production once that particular call happens to reject instead of resolve -- which is exactly the kind of intermittent, hard-to-reproduce failure that makes this mistake worth specifically watching for in code review.

concepts.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
concepts.description: Node shipped its own module system, CommonJS (require/module.exports), years before JavaScript itself standardized ES Modules (import/export) -- Node now supports both, but they differ in loading semantics, scoping, and interop in ways that cause real, specific errors the moment you mix them carelessly.
learningObjectives: Write and consume a module using both CommonJS (require/module.exports) and ES Module (import/export) syntax.
Explain why require() loads synchronously while import loads asynchronously, and connect that back to when each system was designed.
Configure a project to use ES Modules via package.json's type field or explicit .mjs/.cjs extensions.
Identify which CommonJS-only globals (__dirname, __filename, require) are missing in ESM and how to reconstruct their equivalents.
Diagnose the ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error and other common interop failures when CommonJS and ESM code meet in the same project.

sections.heading: Two Systems, One Runtime
Synchronous Loading vs Asynchronous, Static Loading
sections.body:
require() is, deliberately, a **synchronous** function call. When your code hits require('./math'), Node stops, reads that file from disk right there, executes its top-level code immediately, and returns module.exports -- all before your next line of code runs. This was a completely reasonable design in 2009: Promises didn't exist yet in JavaScript, and a synchronous 'load and return the value' model is about as simple as a module system can get. A direct consequence: you can require() conditionally, inside an if, inside a function, computed with a dynamic string -- it's just a normal function call that happens to have a side effect of loading code.

import, by contrast, is **not** a normal function call -- it's a declaration, and the ES Module system is designed to statically analyze a module's entire dependency graph *before running any of the modules' code*, resolving and loading everything asynchronously. This is why import statements must appear at the top level of a file (never inside an if or a function) and why the specifiers must be literal strings in the standard form -- the whole point is that a tool can figure out the complete dependency graph just by reading the file, without executing anything, which is exactly what enables optimizations like dead-code elimination ('tree-shaking') in bundlers, and what allows import resolution to be genuinely asynchronous without your code needing to explicitly wait for it line by line. Node also supports a dynamic, function-like import('./math.js') -- lowercase, with parentheses -- for the genuinely conditional case, and it returns a Promise, which is your signal that this path is asynchronous by design, unlike require.

One more consequence of require's synchronous, immediate-execution model shows up specifically with **circular requires**: if module A requires module B, and B in turn requires A (directly or through a longer chain) before A has finished running its own top-level code, B receives whatever partial module.exports A has built up *so far* -- not the finished version. This is rarely what anyone wants, and it's a distinctly CommonJS problem; ESM's static, pre-resolved graph handles circular imports more gracefully via 'live bindings' that update once the exporting module finishes evaluating.

sections.heading: Configuring and Mixing the Two Systems
Which One Should You Actually Use?
sections.body: For new projects today, ES Modules is the direction the ecosystem and the language itself are moving, and it's a reasonable default choice, particularly since it also unlocks top-level await (using await directly in a module's top-level code, outside any async function, which CommonJS cannot do at all). That said, you will spend a long time working with, and depending on, packages that still ship as CommonJS -- so understanding require()'s behavior, including its synchronous loading and circular-require quirks, remains a practical necessity rather than legacy trivia. The practical rule of thumb: pick one system per project (set it explicitly via package.json's "type" field rather than relying on defaults), be aware that a CJS project's require() cannot pull in an ESM-only dependency without switching to dynamic import(), and don't be surprised when an npm package's documentation shows import syntax that needs translating if your own project is still CommonJS.

examples.title: The Same Module, Written Both Ways
examples.explanation: Both versions produce the identical runtime result, but they get there through entirely different loading mechanisms: the CommonJS version's require call executes synchronously and can omit the file extension, relying on Node's CommonJS resolution algorithm to try .js, .json, and directory-based lookups automatically; the ESM version's import statement is statically resolved before any module code runs, and standard ESM resolution requires the full file extension (./mathUtils.mjs, not ./mathUtils) -- leaving it off is a common early mistake when switching from CommonJS habits. The .mjs extension here also matters on its own: it forces that specific file to be treated as an ES Module regardless of whatever "type" field the nearest package.json has, which is useful for mixing a single ESM file into an otherwise CommonJS project.

examples.title: Circular require() and a Half-Finished module.exports
examples.explanation: require('./a') from main.js starts a.js running immediately and synchronously. a.js sets module.exports.value = 1, then requires b.js, which starts running in turn -- but when b.js requires('./a') partway through its own execution, a.js has not finished yet: it's paused mid-file, waiting on that very require('./b') call. Node does not re-run a.js from the top (that would recurse forever); instead it hands b.js whatever a.js's module.exports currently looks like, which is { value: 1 } -- the assignment value = 2 later in a.js hasn't executed yet. This is precisely why b.js reports a.value as 1, not 2: circular requires don't get a finished module, they get a snapshot of whatever partial state existed at the moment the cycle closed.

examples.title: Recovering __dirname in an ES Module
examples.explanation: import.meta.url gives this specific module's own location as a file:// URL string -- something ESM provides natively as part of the language standard, unlike Node's CommonJS-only __dirname. fileURLToPath (from Node's url core module) converts that URL into an ordinary OS-native filesystem path, and path.dirname strips the filename off, giving the same value __dirname would have held in a CommonJS file. This matters because process.cwd() is not a substitute -- it returns the directory the process happened to be launched *from*, which is very often a different directory than where this particular source file physically lives once a project has any real folder structure, and relying on it for locating a file relative to the module's own source tends to break the moment someone runs the app from a different working directory.

misconceptions.description: require() and import are just two different pieces of syntax for doing the exact same thing under the hood, so which one a file uses is purely a style preference.
misconceptions.clarification: They differ in fundamental ways beyond syntax. require loads and executes synchronously, at the exact call site, and can be called conditionally anywhere in code; import is statically resolved and loaded asynchronously, must appear at a module's top level, and enables tooling (bundling, tree-shaking) that inspects the dependency graph without running any code. They also differ on live bindings: ESM's imported names are live, read-only views onto the exporting module's values that update if the export changes later, while CommonJS's destructured require result is a one-time snapshot copy taken at require time.

misconceptions.description: Since Node supports both module systems, you can require() any ES Module file the same way you require() a CommonJS one, and vice versa, without any special handling.
misconceptions.clarification: The interop is asymmetric. ESM can import a CommonJS module fairly transparently, since Node treats the CJS module's module.exports as its default export. But CommonJS's require() is synchronous and simply cannot load an ESM module at all -- attempting it throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM; the only path from CommonJS to an ESM module is the asynchronous, Promise-returning dynamic import() function, not require().

exercises.prompt: Given these two CommonJS files, what gets logged, and in what order, when main.js runs require('./a')?
hints: Trace execution top to bottom starting from main's require('./a') -- a.js starts running immediately, synchronously, before main.js's next line.
When b.js requires a.js partway through, a.js hasn't finished running yet -- what does Node hand back in that situation: a fully finished module.exports, or whatever a.js has built up so far?
module.exports.value = 1 has already run in a.js before it requires b.js -- so that partial value IS visible to b.js, even though a.js's LATER line (value = 2) hasn't executed yet at that point.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'a.js starts', 'b.js starts', 'b.js sees a.value = 1', 'a.js sees b.value = 20', 'main.js sees a.value = 2' -- b.js sees a's partially-built exports (value=1) rather than a's eventual final value of 2.
exercises.solutionExplanation: main.js's require('./a') starts a.js running: it logs 'a.js starts', sets module.exports.value = 1, then calls require('./b'), which starts b.js. b.js logs 'b.js starts', sets its own value to 10, then calls require('./a') -- but a.js is still paused mid-execution at that exact require('./b') line, so Node hands back a.js's current, unfinished exports object, { value: 1 }. b.js logs that as 1, sets its own value to 20, and finishes, returning { value: 20 } back to a.js's require('./b') call. a.js resumes, logs b.value as 20 (b.js's final value, since b.js had already completely finished by the time a.js reads it), sets its own value to 2, and finishes. Finally, main.js's require('./a') call -- which had been waiting this whole time -- resolves to a.js's now-fully-finished exports, { value: 2 }, so main.js logs 2.

exercises.prompt: A CommonJS Node project (no 'type' field in package.json) has this file, and running it with node app.js fails immediately with 'Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module ... not supported'. Find and fix the problem, assuming logger.mjs must stay written as an ES Module.
hints: require() is synchronous. Is loading an ES Module file (.mjs) something require() is actually able to do at all, regardless of what's inside it?
Node provides a different way to load an ES Module from CommonJS code -- one that's asynchronous, and returns something you have to await or .then() rather than getting the exports back immediately.
Since dynamic import() returns a Promise, the code that uses it will need to either live inside an async function, or use .then(), rather than a single synchronous top-level require line.
exercises.solutionExplanation: require() cannot ever load an ES Module -- this is not a bug to be patched around, but a hard limitation rooted in require's synchronous design meeting ESM's inherently asynchronous loading model. The fix is Node's dynamic, lowercase import() function, which is legal to call from CommonJS files too, and which returns a Promise. Because it's asynchronous, it must be awaited (here inside an async main() wrapper function, since top-level await is not available in CommonJS files) rather than assigned directly the way require's result is, but once awaited it gives back the same { log } exports object the static import syntax would have provided in an ESM file.

assessments.prompt: Why can a CommonJS file not require() an ES Module, while an ES Module CAN import a CommonJS module without much trouble?
options: It's an arbitrary restriction Node added; there's no technical reason it couldn't work in both directions.

require() is synchronous and returns its result immediately on the same line, but loading an ES Module is inherently asynchronous -- there's no way to synchronously hand back a result that isn't ready yet. ESM's import (dynamic or static) is asynchronous by design, so it can wait for a CommonJS module's already-synchronous load to finish without any conflict.
CommonJS modules are always smaller in file size, so they load fast enough for import to handle them, while ES Modules are too large for require to process.
ES Modules can only be loaded in a browser, never inside a Node.js process directly.
assessments.explanation: The constraint is a genuine technical one about loading semantics, not an arbitrary rule: require's contract is to hand back a finished result synchronously, on the very same line it's called, and there is fundamentally no way to do that for something that loads asynchronously. Import, by contrast, is asynchronous by design (even its static form resolves before execution but doesn't block a calling line the way require does), so it has no trouble waiting on a CommonJS module's load, which is already synchronous and instant from import's perspective. Option A is wrong because this is a real technical constraint, not an arbitrary one. Option C is wrong -- file size has nothing to do with it; the issue is purely about synchronous vs asynchronous loading contracts. Option D is wrong -- Node has run ESM files directly, with no browser involved, since roughly version 12-13.

assessments.prompt: A .js file lives in a project whose package.json has no "type" field at all. How does Node decide whether to treat that file as CommonJS or an ES Module?
options: Node inspects the file's contents for import/export keywords and automatically picks the matching module system.
Omitting the "type" field defaults to CommonJS, so the .js file is loaded and executed as CommonJS.
Node treats it as an ES Module by default, mirroring how a browser's <script type="module"> behaves.
Node refuses to run the file at all until "type" is set explicitly to either value.
assessments.explanation: Node decides a .js file's module system from the nearest package.json's "type" field, and the documented default when that field is entirely omitted is "commonjs" -- so a plain .js file in a project with no "type" field is loaded as CommonJS, require/module.exports and all. Option A is wrong -- Node does not scan file contents to infer the module system; it relies on the explicit or defaulted "type" field (or the .mjs/.cjs extension). Option C is wrong -- ESM-by-default is not Node's behavior; CommonJS remains the default specifically for backwards compatibility with the enormous pre-existing CommonJS ecosystem. Option D is wrong -- omitting "type" is completely valid and extremely common; it does not block execution.

assessments.prompt: The CommonJS example imports square via require('./mathUtils') (no extension), while the ES Module version needs import { square } from './mathUtils.mjs' (full extension included). Why does ESM require the extension while CommonJS can omit it?
options: It's arbitrary; both systems could equally support either behavior.

CommonJS's require() runs its own resolution algorithm that automatically tries several extensions and directory-based lookups, while standard ES Module resolution requires the full, explicit file extension in the specifier -- there's no equivalent automatic extension-guessing step in ESM.
.mjs files cannot have their extension omitted because they are always precompiled ahead of time, unlike ordinary .js files.
Node only added extension-omission support to CommonJS in a later version, and deliberately never backported it to ESM for security reasons.
assessments.explanation: require()'s resolution algorithm is designed to be forgiving -- it tries appending .js, .json, and checking for a directory with an index file if a bare specifier doesn't resolve directly. ESM's static resolution model has no equivalent step; specifiers must be exact, extension included, which is part of what makes it possible to resolve the whole dependency graph up front without running any code. Option A dismisses a real, documented difference in resolution algorithms. Option C invents a compilation distinction that isn't the actual reason. Option D fabricates a security-motivated history that isn't accurate -- the difference is about resolution algorithm design, not a security feature that was selectively applied.

assessments.prompt: Which statement about recovering __dirname-equivalent behavior inside an ES Module is correct?
options: process.cwd() is a reliable substitute for __dirname, since it always returns the directory containing the currently executing module file.
__dirname is automatically available in ESM files too, since Node injects it as a global regardless of which module system is in use.

import.meta.url gives the current module's own location as a file:// URL string, which fileURLToPath can convert into a native filesystem path, and path.dirname on that result gives the equivalent of __dirname.
There is no way to determine a module's own file location from within an ES Module; the value must be hardcoded or passed in as a parameter.
assessments.explanation: import.meta.url is the ESM-native primitive that exposes a module's own location as a file:// URL. Running it through fileURLToPath (from Node's 'url' core module) converts that URL to an ordinary OS-native path, and path.dirname on the result reconstructs exactly what __dirname would have given in CommonJS. Option A is a common but incorrect assumption -- process.cwd() returns wherever the process happened to be launched from, which is frequently a different directory than where the source file itself lives, and relying on it for file-relative paths breaks the moment the launch directory changes. Option B is wrong -- __dirname is a CommonJS-only convenience that simply doesn't exist in ESM's scope. Option D is wrong -- import.meta.url plus the reconstruction shown is the standard, well-supported idiom for exactly this purpose.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer converted their Node project from CommonJS to ES Modules by changing package.json's 'type' field to 'module' and swapping require/module.exports for import/export. Afterward, every file that used __dirname to build file paths started throwing 'ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined'. Explain what happened and how to fix it properly.
assessments.modelAnswer: __dirname (along with __filename, require, module, and exports) is not part of the JavaScript language's own ES Module specification at all -- it's a convenience Node injects specifically into CommonJS modules, as part of Node's own implementation of that system, not something ECMAScript modules provide. When the project's package.json switched to "type": "module", every plain .js file in that project is now loaded and executed as an ES Module rather than as CommonJS, and Node simply does not define those CommonJS-only globals in that context -- so any code still referencing __dirname immediately throws a ReferenceError, because that name genuinely doesn't exist in an ES Module's scope, not because of some usage mistake. The correct fix is not to try to get __dirname back as-is, but to reconstruct the same information using ESM's own primitive: import.meta.url gives the current module's own location as a file:// URL string; running that through fileURLToPath (from Node's 'url' core module) converts it into an ordinary OS-native filesystem path, and path.dirname on that result gives you the equivalent of __dirname. It's a few extra lines compared to CommonJS's free global, but it's the standard, correct idiom -- and it's worth explaining to the junior developer that this isn't a bug or a gap Node forgot to fill; it's a direct consequence of ESM being a language-level standard that intentionally doesn't bake in Node-specific globals the way Node's own older CommonJS system did.
